clinicalPearls: Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia is the involuntary contraction of the external urethral sphincter during a detrusor contraction, producing functional outlet obstruction, and is a hallmark of suprasacral spinal cord pathology.

It arises from a lesion between the pontine micturition centre and the sacral cord, most commonly spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, transverse myelitis or myelomeningocele; a lesion above the pons does not cause it.
The dangerous consequence is sustained high detrusor storage and voiding pressure, which threatens the upper tracts with vesicoureteric reflux, hydronephrosis and renal failure.
Diagnosis is made by video-urodynamics showing simultaneous detrusor contraction and increased external sphincter electromyographic activity with a characteristic obstructed flow pattern.
Symptoms overlap with mechanical obstruction: hesitancy, interrupted or staccato flow, incomplete emptying and recurrent infection, so urodynamic confirmation is essential before treatment.
Management prioritises conversion of a high-pressure system to a safe low-pressure reservoir, commonly with clean intermittent catheterisation combined with detrusor pressure-lowering therapy.
Chemical relaxation of the sphincter with botulinum toxin, or pharmacological or surgical outlet reduction, may be used, and afferent-modulating neuromodulation is emerging in selected patients.
Lifelong upper tract surveillance is mandatory because renal deterioration can progress silently despite apparently adequate bladder emptying.
reference.pathophysiology: Normal voiding requires coordinated relaxation of the external urethral sphincter at the moment the detrusor contracts, an interaction organised by the pontine micturition centre. When a neurological lesion interrupts the pathways between the pons and the sacral spinal cord, this coordination is lost: the sacral reflex arcs mediating detrusor contraction and sphincter activity become dissociated, so the external sphincter contracts involuntarily during detrusor contraction rather than relaxing. The bladder therefore contracts against a closed or intermittently closing outlet, generating high intravesical pressure with poor and inefficient urine flow. Sustained elevation of storage and voiding pressures produces detrusor wall thickening and reduced compliance, promotes vesicoureteric reflux and impedes ureteric drainage, ultimately endangering renal function. The severity and pattern correlate with the level and completeness of the underlying cord lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Anatomical bladder outlet obstruction (benign prostatic obstruction, urethral stricture)
Fowler's syndrome (impaired sphincter relaxation in young women)
Dysfunctional voiding in neurologically intact patients
additionalInvestigations: Renal function tests and serial upper tract ultrasound
MRI of the spinal cord or brain to define the neurological lesion
Cystoscopy to exclude structural outlet obstruction
Isotope renography to assess differential function and drainage
Urine culture given the high infection risk
redFlags: Rising serum creatinine or new hydronephrosis on surveillance imaging
High detrusor storage or voiding pressure with poor compliance on urodynamics
Recurrent febrile urinary infection or urosepsis
Autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension in high spinal lesions
reference.prognosis: With early urodynamic diagnosis and a management strategy that maintains low storage and voiding pressures, most patients preserve renal function and avoid serious upper tract damage. Untreated or poorly controlled detrusor sphincter dyssynergia carries a substantial long-term risk of progressive renal impairment and recurrent sepsis.
pitfalls: Attributing obstructive symptoms to prostatic enlargement and offering outlet surgery without recognising the neurological dyssynergia
Relying on symptoms or flow rate alone rather than video-urodynamics to confirm the diagnosis
Focusing on continence while neglecting the high storage pressures that threaten the kidneys
Failing to arrange lifelong upper tract surveillance in a neurological bladder
Overlooking autonomic dysreflexia as a life-threatening consequence of bladder distension in cervical or high thoracic lesions
references: European Association of Urology Guidelines on neuro-urology
International Continence Society standardisation of terminology
management: Convert the high-pressure bladder to a safe low-pressure reservoir with clean intermittent catheterisation combined with detrusor pressure-lowering therapy using antimuscarinics or a beta-3 agonist
Intradetrusor botulinum toxin for refractory detrusor overactivity and high storage pressure
Reduce outlet resistance with alpha-blockers, sphincteric botulinum toxin injection, or endoscopic sphincterotomy or a urethral stent in selected men
Treat and prevent recurrent urinary tract infection
Protect the upper tracts with surveillance renal ultrasound, renal function testing and repeat urodynamics
Treat the underlying neurological cause such as multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury alongside the relevant neurology team
Consider urinary diversion or augmentation cystoplasty for refractory high-pressure disease threatening the kidneys, escalating on evidence of hydronephrosis, reflux or deteriorating renal function
